articles.title: Serbia: Student-backed election winners demand sweeping resignations
articles.summary: Days after ousting Aleksandar Vučić's party from power, Student List MPs call for top figures to stand down.
articles.body:
Serbia's victorious student-led movement has called for top figures in the police, intelligence and judiciary to stand down, days after ousting ex-president Aleksandar Vučić's party from power.

Standing in Pioneers' Park opposite parliament, newly elected MPs on the Student List demanded the immediate dismissal of all police officers who had broken the law, singling out the heads of the police, the BIA security agency and anti-terror unit.

It is not often a European country votes to fully reset its political system overnight, and Serbians have voted to hand the task to a group of novice politicians, made up of intellectuals, professors, artists, athletes and as many as 12 medical doctors and surgeons.

But the handover of power will take weeks, and the students' movement is concerned that evidence of possible wrongdoing could be destroyed in that time.

Just a few days ago, the park they were standing in on Thursday was a tent camp, filled with Vučić loyalists outside his office.

Within hours of him admitting defeat on Sunday night, the camp was dismantled, and a team of volunteers moved in on Monday morning to clean up the mess.

"This is just the first wave of spring cleaning, the new ones are coming now - we are very excited but ready to do it too," said Marija Milovanović, 25, as she scrubbed a park bench.

The student movement emerged from protests following the fatal collapse of a railway station canopy that killed 16 people in November 2024, in Serbia's second largest town Novi Sad.

Their desire was to bring those responsible to justice, and investigate widespread corruption claims blamed for one of the most tragic events in Serbia's modern history.

How a movement of students brought down Serbia's Vučić

Celebrations in Serbia after veteran ruler Vučić loses election to student-led protest movement

Under their Student Plan, they promise to "halt the plunder, return stolen goods to the state budget, and invest directly in education and the economy".

The purge of Vučić loyalists has already begun at Serbia's state broadcaster RTS, where director Manja Grčić has stepped down.

Newly elected MP Mirjana Nikolić said Serbian citizens had the right to truthful information and RTS had served the interests of the government for years.

The new MPs have also set their sights on replacing the head of Telekom Srbija, Vladimir Lučić.

Vučić loyalist Ana Brnabić, who is currently Serbia's acting president, has accused her opponents of choosing "revolutionary justice, not rule of law," and of aiming to shut down "all of the media they dislike".

But one of the next government's best-known MPs, Dejan Šoškić, argues that key reforms need to be in place fast.

"In the first six months, I would like to see the media scene liberated, fighting against corruption on the way, the institutions operating as prescribed by laws and a lustration law introduced," said Šoškić, an economist who served as governor of the central bank between 2010 and 2012.

By lustration, he means banning from public office members of the Vučić government or party apparatus who are found to have violated the rights of Serbians.

That kind of purge will take time, as all of Serbia's main pillars of authority have been held by Vučić and his party for so long, warns Strahinja Subotić of Belgrade-based European Policy Centre.

Ultimately, he believes the new administration will have to "build bridges to the segments that have been operating well in the past".

All 141 successful candidates were chosen by students from universities across Serbia through a lengthy, secretive and carefully crafted process, and tasked with implementing the movement's plan for a complete rebuild of the country.

That political agenda took months for a highly diverse group of students to agree to. Now it is up to the equally disparate team of successful candidates to put the plan into practice, rather than the students themselves.

Another prominent figure on the Student List, is Radomir Saičić, a professor of organic chemistry at the University of Belgrade.

"While the practical mechanisms will be developed on the go, the new MPs will stick to the students' 1200-page long and detailed plan," he told the BBC.

"Parliament is making decisions, but since this change was led by students' efforts, we would highly value their opinion and work closely with them," he promised.

Not only are they newcomers to politics, but Serbia's election winners have no obvious leader and are faced with a series of complex challenges, including taking on the country's highly complex balancing act on the international stage.

Serbia is both a candidate to join the European Union and maintains close relations with Russia. Its bid to join the bloc has long been on the back-burner, while its Western Balkan neighbours press ahead.

The EU was quick to welcome the Student List victory and has promised to back their push for reforms to the rule of law, media freedom and fight against corruption.

But EU integration occupies a strikingly minor place in the students' election manifesto, which describes the bloc merely as Serbia's "most important economic partner".

For years, Belgrade has balanced its foreign policy between the EU and its eastern partners, Russia and China. Belgrade has managed to stand out in Europe by not imposing sanctions on Moscow since the start of its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

In return, Serbia has been rewarded with preferential gas prices that have helped maintain domestic stability, and Vladimir Putin publicly endorsed Vučić's bid to remain in power.

That does not mean that the students have any plans to change course, and changing Serbia's foreign policy may not be high on their list.

"Serbia had it own experience with sanctions in the 1990s and we know that they mostly harm ordinary people and do not affect policies of a state," said Dejan Šoškić, referring to UN sanctions imposed during the wars in former Yugoslavia.

The new government's initial focus will most likely be on domestic reform, and the clock is already ticking before the next election campaign, with presidential elections due to take place in December.

Aleksandar Vučić is legally barred from running for a third term as president, but he has promised that his defeated Serbian Progressive Party will fight back: "We will beat them much faster than they can even imagine."

articles.title: Nancy Pelosi calls Mamdani, El-Sayed's past comments on Israel 'concerning' and 'wrong'
articles.summary: Nancy Pelosi called New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Michigan Democrat Abdul El-Sayed's views on Israel "wrong" and not reflective of House Democrats.
articles.body: Former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., criticized New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Michigan Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed over their views on Israel Thursday, calling their positions "wrong" and saying they did not reflect congressional Democrats. The two progressive Democrats were mentioned by "On Brand" podcast host Donny Deutsch, who asked Pelosi how he, as a Jewish man, could reconcile his support for the Democratic Party with politicians whose statements he considered antisemitic. "When you say Israel doesn't have the right to be a Jewish state, that's antisemitic as far as I'm concerned with all that," Deutsch said. PRO-ISRAEL LEADER WARNS DEMOCRATS FAILING TO CONDEMN ‘VICIOUS JEW HATERS’ IN CONGRESS When Pelosi asked for examples, Deutsch named Mamdani and El-Sayed, calling their comments "concerning." "No, it's more than concerning," Pelosi responded. "It's wrong. It's wrong. And it isn't a reflection of the Democrats in the Congress of the United States. This new person in Michigan, we'll see if he gets elected to the Congress. But the mayor, bless his heart, I hope he succeeds as mayor, but I don't agree with some of the things he has said. But in terms of our people in the House of Representatives, if somebody says that, the other members disassociate themselves from it." Before he was elected New York City mayor, Mamdani repeatedly dodged questions when asked if Israel should be a Jewish state. In a June 28 interview with ABC News, however, Mamdani said he supported Israel as a state with equal rights but declined to endorse it as a Jewish state. "I think any state that privileges one religion over the other is one that I can’t tell you I support, whether it be Israel or Saudi Arabia or anywhere else," Mamdani said. El-Sayed has repeatedly declined to affirm whether Israel has the right to exist as a Jewish state. In a May appearance with Jewish supporters, the candidate said he "struggled" to answer this question and suggested the idea of a Jewish state wasn't consistent with the liberal values "we say we believe in here in the United States." CARVILLE WARNS DEMOCRATS' ANTI-ISRAEL ‘LOUDMOUTHS’ COULD COST ELECTIONS Earlier in the interview with Deutsch, Pelosi initially denied that anyone in the Democratic Party was antisemitic. "The fact is that I really do not know of anybody there on our side who is engaged in antisemitism. That may be what it appears to be or what they're charged to be. But if they are, it's only a few. If there are, I think sometimes they say things that they shouldn't and can be interpreted that way," Pelosi said. Despite her concerns about Mamdani and El-Sayed's comments, she dismissed their impact on the party as a whole. "People represent their districts, and we have to respect that. The job description, job title is representative, but that doesn't mean it has an impact on the consensus of the Democratic Party, and [House Minority Leader] Hakeem Jeffries has been very clear on that," Pelosi said. Fox News Digital reached out to representatives for Pelosi, Mamdani and El-Sayed for comment but did not immediately receive a response. RAHM EMANUEL ACCUSES ANTI-ISRAEL DEMS OF HAVING NO MIDDLE EAST PLAN BESIDES CUTTING FUNDING TO JEWISH STATE Rabbi Yaakov Menken, executive vice president of the Coalition for Jewish Values, acknowledged Pelosi "as one of the Jewish community's best friends among House Democrats" but said it was alarming that she did not seem to recognize antisemitism among her colleagues. If she is indeed one of our best friends, should we not be scared by that?" Menken told Fox News Digital.

articles.title: I didn't know when I collapsed at work - it was low vitamin D
articles.summary: Doctors are finding vitamin D deficiency is increasingly widespread in the UK, especially in young people. But the symptoms are difficult to spot and can be missed.
articles.body:
Twenty-three-year-old Saskia Reeves-Priestley was at work when she suddenly collapsed.

"I just felt really dizzy, really nauseous, was having heart palpitations and was really hot," she says.

There had been no prior warning. Saskia, a special educational needs teacher, was a keen goalkeeper who played football four times a week and felt fit and healthy.

She would later be diagnosed as vitamin D-deficient – blood tests showed her levels were "next to nothing".

In the UK, low vitamin rates are increasing in some age groups - particularly in girls and young women.

According to data from the National Diet and Nutrition Survey, last year nearly a quarter of 11- to 18-year-olds were classed as deficient.

Vitamin D can come from our diet, in foods such as oily fish and meat, or supplements.

But most is made by our body when UV light in sunlight hits the skin. Lower levels of sunlight - depending on where in the world you live or the time of year - decrease the body's ability to produce it.

Covering parts of the body and wearing sunscreen also has an impact - despite their protective advantages.

Those with darker skin need exposure to stronger light to produce the same amount of vitamin D as lighter skin.

Doctors don't routinely offer blood tests to check for vitamin D deficiency, but will offer a supplement if a patient is concerned they might be high risk.

What are the symptoms - and their daily impact?

Vitamin D deficiency is linked to the bone disease rickets in babies and infants. In adults it causes a similar weakening of the bone called osteomalacia .

"They call it the silent disease," says Dr Suma Uday, a paediatric endocrinologist who wants to raise awareness of the problem.

She warns that vitamin D deficiency in young people and adults is difficult to spot and can be missed or misdiagnosed. Symptoms include fatigue and joint and bone pain.

Uday says: "It's basically silently eating away at the bones, leaving them softened and prone to breaks."

Amaka was in the middle of making dinner at her university house in Liverpool when she started shaking.

"I couldn't really see in front of me," she says. Her housemate took her to A&E - later she too would be diagnosed as vitamin D deficient.

Other than feeling tired, she says she had no symptoms: "I'm a 21-year-old student. I've got work and uni - I'm always feeling tired."

She remembers her mother suffering from low vitamin D but says she did not realise it could happen to her.

After taking supplements, Amaka feels a lot better, but she is anxious in case it happens again. "It was scary and I don't want to experience that again."

Uday joins other clinicians and academics who have formed a group - ACT NOW Vitamin D - calling for the threshold at which you are classified as deficient to be raised.

She says that would "catch" more people with low vitamin D and give a more accurate picture of how widespread the issue is. It would also mean they can treat the deficiency earlier, she says.

Uday warns of "a lifelong deficit" in women - in adolescence, then pregnancy, and then the newborn is affected.

"If you don't correct it from the very beginning," she says, "this is going to affect multiple generations."

"It's shocking," says Prof Martin Hewison, from the University of Birmingham.

He tells me that despite being 100 years on from the discovery of vitamin D "rickets hasn't gone away".

"If we have rickets in the community, there are going to be many more people who are vitamin D deficient."

He says the government should look into wider fortification of food in which vitamins are added to foods during production. Countries like Canada and Sweden have mandatory policies.

In the UK, some foods such as breakfast cereals and spreads are already fortified with vitamin D, but it is voluntary.

During the winter months, people start to lose their vitamin D levels.

"We might have to accept that for certain groups vitamin D supplementation is a matter of course," says Hewison.

Saskia is now taking vitamin D supplements regularly - and is back in goal.

articles.title: Taylor Swift gave $100,000 to revive a Tennessee playground destroyed by floods in 2010, now the city is seeking a roughly $3 million grant for an inclusive play area and sports upgrades at the same park
articles.summary: Taylor Swift, the iconic American singer and songwriter.
articles.body: Taylor Swift, the iconic American singer and songwriter. keeps making headlines not only for her songs but also for the tremendous charity works that she keeps doing. This time, the 14 Grammy winner is again in the news for her charity work for kids. In 2010, when devastating floods damaged a popular playground in Hendersonville, Tennessee, Swift contributed $100,000 to help bring it back to life.Now 16 years later, the playground, known as Kids Kingdom, has returned to the spotlight as the city considers a fresh investment in recreational facilities. It includes an all-inclusive playground and better sports field.In August 2026, Hendersonville officials discussed applying for a grant of approximately $3 million through the BlueCross BlueShield of Tennessee Healthy Place programme. The proposed funding would support an all-inclusive playground at Taylor Swift’s Kids Kingdom and turf improvements at Memorial Park’s lacrosse field.This new development has brought renewed attention to a community playground being supported by the singer.What happened in 2010Kids Kingdom was originally built in 1996 as a community-wide project in Hendersonville, a city near Nashville where Swift went to high school. More than 1,500 volunteers reportedly helped construct the original playground. However, the playground's location made it vulnerable to flooding.In May 2010, heavy rainfall caused the Cumberland River to overflow and the water rose to 52 feet. It damaged Hendersonville, where Kids Kingdom was left with serious safety problems.Although the playground had experienced flooding before, the 2010’s was a disaster. As per to playground manufacturer Little Tikes Commercial, Tennessee's parks and recreation authorities considered the facility too dangerous to remain open in its existing condition.The $100,000 donation for the renovation of the playWhile the estimated cost of rebuilding the playground was $175,000, funding constraints threatened to delay the reconstruction work. Swift, who had grown up in Hendersonville, came forward and donated $100,000 for the work. Contemporary reports published in August 2010 confirmed that the singer had donated the money.As per a report by Little Tikes Commercial, her contribution was significant and helped the city bridge the funding gap and move ahead with rebuilding the damaged facility. The donation helped restore a shared community space.In December 2009, she had donated $250,000 to support schools she had attended. She also contributed $500,000 towards flood relief efforts in the Nashville area in 2010, according to local reports.Preserving the playground's identityThe rebuilt playground preserved its castle theme, and colourful structures, spiral staircases and modern play equipment were added. Its distinctive arched entrance was also retained, keeping it original.Plans included plaques recognising the 1,500 people who had helped construct the original facility, along with clay handprints made by children. For Hendersonville residents, the playground represented not simply a recreational space but also a place created through collective effort.Why Hendersonville is considering another investmentThe proposed 2026 grant would focus on making recreational spaces. An all-inclusive playground is designed to enable children with different abilities to play together. Depending on its final design, such a facility can incorporate accessible routes.According to the published summary of Hendersonville's committee discussions, the proposed grant would not require a local matching contribution. However, the funding remained subject to the grant application process, and the available records did not confirm a final award.For Hendersonville, the story of Kids Kingdom has come full circle in an important way. A playground that was built through community participation was severely damaged by flooding, then rebuilt with help from a hometown celebrity.Swift's $100,000 donation helped make that reconstruction possible in 2010. Now, the city's proposed grant application places the same playground at the centre of another effort to improve public recreation.Whether the latest funding bid succeeds remains to be seen. articles.title: Biggest fibre boost could be scraps in your bin, experts say
articles.summary: Chomping on vegtable skins, seeds and stalks could give us vital fibre, say food scientists.
articles.body:
Eating fruit and vegetable scraps such as peels and stalks could provide a health boost that most of us are missing, say UK researchers .

They say scraps are an overlooked source of dietary fibre and are encouraging people to try "root-to-tip" eating, including watermelon rind, pineapple core and butternut squash seeds.

Most adults do not get enough fibre. Official figures show only 4% meet the recommended 30g a day, despite its well-known benefits for gut health.

Fibre aids digestion, helps you feel fuller for longer and is linked to a lower risk of heart disease and bowel cancer.

As a rule of thumb, the skins of fruit and veg pack more fibre than the insides.

Eating a kiwi with the skin on provides 50% more fibre than having a peeled one, for example.

For their study, the scientists at King's College London analysed 12 raw or uncooked fresh foods - beetroot, bell pepper, broccoli, butternut squash, cauliflower, celeriac, curly kale, fennel, kiwi fruit, leek, pineapple and watermelon.

They found many discarded parts contained more fibre than the sections people typically eat.

watermelon rind contained 2.10g of fibre per 100g – roughly equivalent to the fibre in a slice of wholemeal bread

butternut squash skin and seeds contained 9.25g per 100g – nearly as much fibre as a bowl of bran flakes

pineapple skin and core contained five times more fibre than the flesh

broccoli stalks contained fibre, although a bit less than the florets

Fibre is essential for your gut to work properly and helps prevent constipation.

Project lead Dr Rachel Gibson said the findings suggested people are throwing away a significant amount of fibre.

"This isn't just a nutritional loss, it's also a financial one; you're effectively throwing away a substantial portion of what you've paid for."

The college has been experimenting in its canteen , offering staff and students root-to-tip meals, such as banana skin curry.

At home, people might want to try leaving skins on kiwi fruit, using broccoli stalks in stir-fries, or adding bell pepper seeds to dishes, the researchers suggest.

While cooking can change the fibre content, it doesn't usually destroy it all.

Steaming, microwaving, or quick sautéing tends to preserve nutrients best .

Dr Gibson said: "This isn't about perfection and this isn't about forcing people to eat unpalatable food – it's about recognising the nutritional value in components we've been conditioned to discard."

She acknowledges some may be hesitant to try.

Some diners raised concerns during the canteen trial.

Over the nine-week period, 'root-to-tip' dishes made up a third of total daily hot menu sales at the university.

Those choosing the new dishes were less likely to finish their meals than diners eating from the conventional menu.

Kirsten Jackson, a dietitian with the British Dietetic Association who specialises in irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), says the food hacks are useful as long as produce is washed thoroughly.

She suggests blending pineapple cores into smoothies, but says the tough skins are not something she would recommend.

Some stalks may need to be cooked or finely chopped to make them more palatable, she adds.

"Just because a broccoli stalk doesn't fit into tonight's meal doesn't mean it needs to go in the bin. Chop it up, freeze it and add it to a soup or stir-fry another day," she said.

She advises increasing fibre intake gradually to avoid bloating, noting that people with IBS may find it harder to tolerate.

And there are some things to avoid entirely, said the British Nutrition Foundation.

Green potatoes and rhubarb leaves contain toxic compounds, while tough stalks and seeds may not be suitable for young children.

articles.title: EU force helicopter crash kills four in Bosnia
articles.summary: EUFOR confirms CH-47 Chinook helicopter crash in Bosnia, with four Italian nationals confirmed dead.
articles.body:
Four people belonging to the European Union Force in Bosnia ( EUFOR ) have been killed after an Italian military helicopter conducting a training operation crashed.

EUFOR said a CH-47 Chinook helicopter crashed during “routine training” in the Brcko region on Thursday, about 180km (110 miles) north of Bosnia’s capital, Sarajevo.

A total of 11 people were injured in the crash, EUFOR said, adding that all the injured are receiving treatment and are in stable condition.

The Italian government said in a statement that all those on board the military helicopter were its nationals.

The victims were two soldiers and two Red Cross volunteers, according to the Italian defence ministry.

“At this moment of immense grief, my thoughts go first and foremost to the families of our fallen, to whom I extend my personal condolences and those of the entire defence establishment,” Italian Defence Minister Guido Crosetto said.

Bosnian media outlets published photos of the wreckage showing the helicopter overturned on the ground in a flat field.

A spokesman for Brcko hospital told the AFP news agency that there were 15 people on board at the time of the crash, which initially killed three people.

“Twelve people were transported to our hospital. Unfortunately, a fourth person succumbed to injuries in the hospital,” the spokesman said.

“EUFOR is conducting a full and thorough investigation of the incident and will release more information as it is verified, and when appropriate,” the force said in a statement.

EUFOR, which has between 1,000 and 1,500 personnel, has been deployed in Bosnia since 2004, when it replaced a NATO peacekeeping force that had been in the country since the Bosnian War ended in 1995. The mission oversees the implementation of the Dayton Peace Agreement, which ended the three-year war.

articles.body: A group of Arizona bank employees sprang into action to help a longtime neighborhood food vendor escape a powerful storm, pulling him and his cart inside as strong winds and hail battered the Phoenix area in a heartwarming rescue caught on video. The incident occurred at a PNC Bank branch as severe weather swept through the Phoenix area last week, prompting employees to help a local vendor caught in the storm, according to FOX 10 Phoenix. Video posted by an individual inside the bank shows an employee helping the vendor, identified as Hilario Cruz Cruz, pull his food cart inside as wind and hail batter the area. ARIZONA SHERIFF'S HELICOPTER CREW RESCUES MAN STRANDED ATOP OVERTURNED TRUCK IN RAPIDLY RISING FLOODWATERS "With one hand, I held the door against the strong wind blowing it, and with my other hand I pulled the cart inside. 'WE COULDN'T MAKE PAYROLL': DOUGHNUT SHOP OWNER ASKED GOD FOR HELP — WHAT HAPPENED NEXT STUNNED HIM A week later, however, he was back selling elotes and fresh fruit along Peoria Avenue. articles.title: We went on holiday with our neighbours and swapped families - it tore us apart
articles.summary: Rachel Stone tells how her parents swapped partners, the chaos it caused and how she came to forgive them.
articles.body:
Rachel Stone was five and her brother Ian was 10 when their mum and dad took them on a caravan holiday to Wales with the family next door.

They spent two fun-filled weeks together - but when they got home, each family split in half and swapped houses.

Rachel and her mother Kay moved in with the neighbour Eddie and his daughter Alison. Eddie's wife Irene and their daughter Dawn moved in with Rachel's dad Rex and her brother Ian.

Rachel tells Dr Sian Williams, host of Radio 4's Life Changing podcast, of the trauma of her family being torn apart, the chaos that unfolded and how she has come to forgive her parents.

Rachel and Ian had initially been delighted when a new family moved in next door. "We instantly hit it off, all four of us." They were thrilled to be going on holiday together.

Rachel remembers two caravans parked side-by-side and a trip up Mount Snowdon.

But when it was time to go home, everything was mixed up - people were getting in the wrong cars.

Rachel remembers her mum leaning back from the passenger seat, saying: "'We're going to have a new family. We're going to be living in number eight with Eddie and Alison. Alison's going to be your new sister.

"And your dad and brother are still going to live in number 10. And Auntie Irene and Dawn are going to live there. And Dawn's going to be your brother's new sister."

Rachel immediately felt "very panicked and afraid and upset" and says she started to cry.

As the car rumbled along, she felt "bewildered, but also a little bit excited". She liked Alison and had always wanted a sister.

That night, Alison let her sleep on her top bunk and the next morning the adults switched belongings between the houses in the Isle of Sheppey where they lived.

Rachel says she felt very confused. "You can't help but think that it's your fault."

Life at number 8, where Rachel now lived, was very different to number 10. Her old house had been clean, whereas this house had "dog hair, greasy things, car things".

She describes her mum as "firm but fair" and very practical.

Her stepdad Eddie "was never horrible to me, but I never called him dad. I wasn't his girl."

She also missed Ian desperately. "I was very proud of him. He was my big brother.

"I used to wait in the front garden for him to come home from school when I was a toddler."

Rachel was seven when the two couples went to court together and got divorced. They later married their new partners in separate low-key registry office ceremonies.

Rachel did not even know her dad had married Irene until she saw the wedding photo. Her visits to her old home tailed off when she was about 11 or 12. She says she found it difficult to go and visit her dad and did not get along with Irene.

Meanwhile, life with her mum Kay and Eddie was chaotic.

"[He] was quite possessive and controlling. By the time we got to 13, she [Mum] said, 'it's not sustainable, [we] can't live like this".

Rachel said school was her "escape". She got good grades and became a teacher. She got married and had two sons but is now separated and works as a business coach.

Throughout her life, Rachel's mother would never talk about the swap. "I asked a lot of questions. She told me it was complicated."

Decades later, on a family holiday with her own sons, Rachel asked again.

"I said to my mum, 'Oh, Joseph's 10 now... Ian was 10 when you let him go with Dad and Irene.'"

She says her mum was "beside herself with guilt and the shame... for her selfish decisions"

"Years later she actually said to me - the words I almost wanted to hear all my life - 'I'm so sorry I let you down and I want to try and make it up to you.'"

Rachel says it was the start of her rebuilding a "wonderful" relationship with her mum.

Rachel never had a close relationship with her dad. "He told me he had a choice between his wife and his children. Unfortunately for me, he chose his wife."

He and Irene stayed together until his death aged 81.

But when she spoke at her dad's funeral, Rachel said she felt she owed him an apology.

"I imagined a character of a perfect dad that had been taken away from me... I created this superhuman being that could be everything.

"And I wanted him to be like that. But I also think you have to accept people for who they are.

"I think that parents do the best they can... You can't hope for your parents to be something they're not."

articles.title: Erin Patterson: Australian mushroom murderer loses appeal to overturn convictions
articles.summary: Erin Patterson argued her trial was unfair due to seven grounds but three appeal judges dismissed them all.
articles.body:
Australia's mushroom killer has failed to overturn her murder convictions on appeal, with the court also ruling that she never be released from prison.

Erin Patterson, 52, was found guilty of murdering three relatives and attempting to kill another when she served them a toxic mushroom-laced meal in 2023. Her life sentence included a non-parole period of 33 years.

In Victoria's Court of Appeal on Friday, three judges threw out her appeal against her convictions and agreed with the prosecution that her sentence was inadequate, as it allowed for the possibility of freedom.

Patterson's crimes were "extraordinarily cold and calculated" and had to be "denounced in the strongest terms," they said.

"We have concluded that the case involved such shocking criminality that it is inappropriate to fix a non-parole period," Justice Stephen McLeish told the court, on the panel's behalf.

After a high-profile trial last year, a jury found Patterson guilty of murdering her in-laws, Don and Gail Patterson, and Gail's sister Heather Wilkinson, by serving them individual portions of beef Wellington containing death cap mushrooms.

Patterson was also found guilty of the attempted murder of Heather's husband Ian Wilkinson, a local pastor, who also ate the toxic lunch at Patterson's home in rural Victoria.

He survived after spending weeks in hospital and has ongoing health issues due to the poisoning.

Simon Patterson, the host's estranged husband, was meant to attend the lunch but cancelled at the last minute, in part due to his belief that his wife had repeatedly tried to poison him over several years.

Patterson was sentenced last September , with the trial judge allowing a non-parole period of 33 years due to the "harsh prison conditions" she would likely face.

She promptly launched an appeal against her convictions , with her legal team in August arguing seven grounds for her appeal.

They claimed a hotel booking mishap - which saw the jury stay in the same place as the prosecution, a key police witness and the media - was "catastrophic" and undermined the integrity of her trial.

They also argued certain pieces of evidence shown to the jury were irrelevant and prejudicial - such as cell tower data suggesting Patterson visited areas where death cap mushrooms might be found and Facebook posts where she complained about her in-laws.

Meanwhile, the judge wrongly blocked other evidence that would have demonstrated the mother-of-two's long-time hobby of mushroom foraging, they said.

The defence team also asserted that the prosecution's five-day cross-examination of Patterson was "unfair and oppressive", and that the Crown was inconsistent in its arguments about a motive.

On Friday, the appeal judges dismissed all seven grounds.

Patterson has 28 days to decide if she will seek to convince the High Court of Australia to hear another appeal over the case.

articles.title: Three dead after two helicopters collide midair near Oregon airport
articles.summary: The collision involving a Robinson R22 and an Airbus helicopter occurred on Thursday afternoon, with both aircraft crashing in a field adjacent to a highway.
articles.body:
Three people have died after two helicopters collided midair near a small airport in Oregon, officials said.

The collision involving a Robinson R22 and an Airbus helicopter occurred near McMinnville Municipal Airport on Thursday afternoon. Both aircraft crashed in a field adjacent to a highway, the sheriff's office said.

Authorities identified the victims as a 22-year-old flight instructor from Texas and a student pilot from the United Kingdom, who were aboard one of the helicopters. The sole occupant of the other aircraft was also killed.

I t was not immediately clear what caused the crash.

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) and the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) responded to the scene and are leading the ongoing investigation.

The BBC has contacted the FAA for comment.

The flight instructor on the Robinson R22 was identified Maddie Aasbo. The student pilot from the UK has not yet been publicly identified, as authorities work with the consulate and the FBI to notify the next of kin.

The sole occupant of the Airbus was identified as Tyler Delane Sturdevant, 38, of Newberg, Oregon.

One of the aircraft was operated by Jerry Trimble Helicopters, a flight training school based at the McMinnville Municipal Airport, according to a statement from the company.

"Jerry Trimble Helicopters is deeply saddened to confirm that one of our aircraft was involved in an aviation incident this afternoon," the company said, adding that they were fully cooperating with investigators.

Authorities asked the public to avoid the area as they responded to the incident.

articles.title: Salvadoran ex-president Saca released after 10-year sentence for corruption
articles.summary: Elias Antonio Saca confessed to diverting more than $300m in public funds during his presidency and accepted a plea barg
articles.body:
Elias Antonio Saca, the former president of El Salvador , has been released after serving a 10-year prison term for corruption.

Saca, 61, arrived at court to formally report his release on Thursday after fulfilling the terms of a plea deal in which he confessed to diverting and laundering more than $300m from public funds during his 2004 to 2009 administration.

His lawyer, Mario Machado, said the former president had served his sentence in full without receiving early-release benefits.

Saca was first arrested during his son’s wedding in 2016 and was sentenced to five years for embezzlement and another five years for money laundering in September 2018.

A plea bargain allowed Saca to avoid a potential 30-year prison sentence.

In 2019, the former president was found guilty of offering $10,000 to a court employee to obtain information about a case against him, though a judge determined the second sentence to be part of his existing 10-year term.

Saca, a businessman and radio broadcaster, served as president as part of the right-wing Nationalist Republican Alliance (ARENA).

During the initial trial, prosecutors said Saca appropriated funds from the state budget for himself and others, including taking more than $7m for his former party.

Saca was also ordered to repay $260m to the state. He is one of four Salvadoran presidents who have faced corruption charges, including his successor Mauricio Funes, who escaped to Nicaragua in September 2016 and died there in 2025.

articles.title: Australian court orders Erin Patterson never to be released from prison for mushroom poisonings
articles.summary: Judges said the “shocking criminality” of the case made parole inappropriate for Patterson.
articles.body: MELBOURNE, Australia — An Australian appeals court on Friday ordered triple-murderer Erin Patterson to never be released from prison because of the “shocking criminality” involved in poisoning four of her estranged husband’s relatives with death cap mushrooms. The three judges of the Victoria state Court of Appeal dismissed Patterson’s appeal of her convictions and upheld prosecutors’ challenge to the leniency of her 33-year nonparole sentence, meaning she will spend the rest of her life behind bars. Beforehand, she would have been 82 years old when she could be considered for release. “This offending was extraordinarily cold and calculated and stands to be denounced in the strongest terms,” Justice Stephen McLeish said on behalf of all three judges. “In all the circumstances after anxious consideration, we have concluded that the case involved such shocking criminality that it is inappropriate to fix a nonparole period,” McLeish added. The convictions stemmed from a family meal Patterson hosted at her rural home in Leongatha in July 2023. She can apply to Australia’s High Court to overturn the verdicts on her sentence and her convictions. The High Court is her last appeal option. Patterson insisted that she added death cap mushrooms to the beef Wellington pastry dishes accidentally. She was sentenced last year to three life sentences for murder and 25 years for attempted murder. The deaths of Patterson’s parents-in-law, Don and Gail Patterson, and Gail’s sister, Heather Wilkinson, within days of having lunch immediately attracted an extraordinary level of global media attention. The case has also inspired podcasts, books and screen adaptations. Heather’s husband, Ian Wilkinson, survived the lunch after spending weeks in hospital. Erin Patterson was convicted of his attempted murder. Prosecutors argued at an appeal hearing in August that she should never become eligible for parole. They argued that the minimum period behind bars did not reflect the “calculated criminality” of the case. McLeish said Patterson’s intent to murder all four was sustained for almost three weeks from when she invited them to lunch. Her crimes involved an “elaborate series of deceptions” including falsely claiming a cancer diagnosis to explain the absences of her two children from the lunch, the judge said. The only survivor, Ian Wilkinson, testified that Erin Patterson had told her guests she wanted their advice about what to tell the children about her diagnosis. McLeish noted that Erin Patterson had destroyed evidence, denied foraging for mushrooms and repeatedly made false claims about where the mushrooms had come from. “The offending was carefully planned and deliberate. It represented a cruel breach of trust,” McLeish said. Patterson opted not to attend court and watched the verdicts by video link from prison. Because of her notoriety, Patterson is held in the high-security Gordon Unit of Melbourne’s Dame Phyllis Frost Centre women’s prison. The unit is for prisoners assessed as being at high risk from other inmates. In sentencing her in September 2025, trial judge Christopher Bale said there was a “substantial chance” that Patterson could be held in “solitary confinement for years to come.” Patterson’s estranged husband, Simon Patterson, was invited to the lunch but declined the day before. After her conviction, pretrial evidence was released that detailed the husband’s suspicion that Erin Patterson had previously attempted to kill him. Simon Patterson testified at a pretrial hearing that he had declined the lunch invitation out of fear.

articles.title: Flash floods kill five in Syria
articles.summary: Four children drowned while a man died after his car was caught in floodwaters.
articles.body:
Heavy rains have been pouring over several Syrian provinces, leaving at least five people dead, including four children, in northern and eastern regions.

The four children all drowned in bodies of water across Raqqa and Deir Az Zor governorates, the Ministry of Emergency and Disaster Management said in a statement on Thursday.

A man also died when his car was caught in floodwaters near al-Salmani Bridge in the western Raqqa countryside.

Five others, including two children, remain missing in the storms that have drenched the country.

Thursday marked the second day the ministry recorded responses to flooding across the country. It continues to issue situation updates on its X account.

The ministry reported infrastructure damage and disruptions to several bridges in affected areas: Aleppo, Raqqa, Deir Az Zor, Hasakah and Homs.

State news agency SANA said al-Salmani Bridge, west of Tabqa, collapsed in the flooding, shutting the road linking Raqqa to Aleppo.

Emergency teams also reported rescuing 15 civilians whose vehicles were trapped by floodwaters. The ministry said it evacuated approximately 375 families from three camps on the rural outskirts of Raqqa.

This is not the first time the country has faced the threat of heavy rains and the flooding that follows.

UNICEF reported in June that 17,000 people had been adversely affected by flooding so far in the year. At the time, the UN agency said 700 families had been displaced, including around 2,000 children, and that 49 water treatment plants in Deir Az Zor and Raqqa governorates had also gone out of service.

articles.title: New York police will investigate all sex crimes at Cornell, governor says
articles.summary: The change was announced amid backlash over the school's handling of gang rape allegations involving a fraternity on campus.
articles.body:
New York Governor Kathy Hochul has announced that state police will now investigate all future sexual offence complaints at Cornell University after the fallout from a gang rape accusation at the institution.

It follows the handling of a 2024 alleged campus rape incident, where a student, known anonymously as Jane Doe, filed a lawsuit against Cornell after she was allegedly drugged and gang raped at a fraternity.

The university, after initially defending its disciplinary measures, acknowledged it fell short in its handling of her case.

The fallout has continued to rile the university. Cornell's administration - including its president - is facing a no-confidence vote by its faculty.

Watch: New York governor blasts handling of Cornell rape inquiry

Hochul said New York State Police signed an agreement with Cornell University so that all sexual offence complaints, which had historically fallen under the jurisdiction of university police, will be immediately referred to state police instead.

"When someone reports sexual assault," Hochul said on Thursday, they deserve "to know their allegations will be taken seriously and thoroughly investigated by law enforcement trained to support survivors".

"Survivors should be able to trust the institutions responsible for protecting them," the governor added.

Backlash against the Ivy League university has been intense since Jane Doe filed her lawsuit in mid-September.

On Wednesday, the institution's Faculty Senate, a governing body composed of professors and other academic staff, met behind closed-doors and decided to move forward with voting on a resolution of no-confidence against the administration and the university's President Michael Kotlikoff.

The vote will be open for faculty starting on Friday and run until 6 November. The vote is largely symbolic but could intensify pressure on changing the university's leadership.

Earlier this month, the university announced a series of measures responding to the alleged assault, including adding sexual assault investigators to its police force.

Hochul had said she was "deeply disturbed" by how the investigation was handled. She appointed a special prosecutor , New York's Attorney General Letitia James, earlier this month to oversee a reopened investigation into whether criminal charges are warranted.

The woman at the centre of the case filed a civil lawsuit alleging that she was drugged and raped by seven men at a fraternity house at the university in 2024.

She claimed that Cornell failed to protect her or adequately punish the men, who have now become known as the Cornell Seven.

articles.title: Protests and violence now go hand in hand in France. It wasn’t always like this
articles.summary: Lucas Petit was just 11 when hundreds of thousands of men and women wearing yellow vests poured onto the streets and occupied roundabouts across France in November 2018.
articles.body: Lucas Petit was just 11 when hundreds of thousands of men and women wearing yellow vests poured onto the streets and occupied roundabouts across France in November 2018. His memories are hazy, though stories of clashes with police left a lasting impression. If he ever joined a demonstration, he knew what to expect. “It helped shape this whole collective image of a violent protest,” he told CNN. Petit, now 19, belongs to a generation for whom tear gas, water cannons, rubber bullets and stun grenades are par for the course when protesting. “We feel somewhat compelled to respond with violence because we’re facing social, institutional, symbolic and now physical oppression,” Petit said. “So I think violence has become normalized.” Petit has been blockading his school in eastern Paris for more than a month. He’s part of a movement that started out demanding better conditions at French schools and has since swelled into a collective cry of anger, bringing together groups with different grievances. On October 17, a day of largely peaceful nationwide protests morphed into chaotic scenes of looting and destruction: Limoges’s historic town hall went up in flames; shops were ransacked, and protesters were maimed for life. Opportunistic looters joined in, alongside young protesters from various backgrounds. According to an internal Justice Ministry document, 68% of the 186 people jailed between October 18 and 21 were 25 or younger, while 52% had no previous criminal record. Nearly half were classified as looters. Failures in the police response help explain how the situation got so out of control. Behind the tear gas and smoke, however, lies a shift in how some French protesters operate. Over the past decade, some have developed a savoir-faire for confrontation. As riot police have adapted their tactics and weapons, demonstrators have become adept at anticipating police maneuvers and exploiting gaps in security. Methods once associated with organized radical militants have spread to a younger generation. How Black Bloc tactics spread They tend to gather at the front of demonstrations, dressed head to toe in black, masked and hooded earning them the moniker “Black Bloc.” The groups first appeared in Germany in the 1980s. Associated with anarchist and anti-capitalist movements, Black Bloc is not an organization with a formal leadership; it’s a set of protest tactics. These methods gained prominence in France during the 2016 labor protests before spreading further during the Yellow Vest movement. Identities are concealed and participants often act as a group, sometimes attacking symbols of capitalism such as luxury stores. These type of protesters are often referred to as “casseurs” too, from the verb “casser,” meaning “to break” – a broad term that can be applied to anyone who vandalizes property regardless of their ideological beliefs. “Many young people who aren’t originally from the ultra-left are now adopting Black Bloc tactics,” said Thierry Vincent, an expert on radical-left movements. “It’s a way of protesting that doesn’t shock many young people anymore.” One Black Bloc tactic involves small, highly mobile groups breaking away from the main march, forcing police to spread their forces thin, making it harder for them to respond in a coordinated way. That was on display a fortnight ago when a group of protesters attempted to reach the Elysee Palace, drawing riot police away from the demonstration. The maneuver worked. Police resources were stretched, and it contributed to officers being overwhelmed that day. It’s not just their methods that have caught on. There’s also a wider willingness to confront the police. Hugo Melchior, a historian and left-wing activist who has attended demonstrations in the northwestern city of Rennes for two decades, saw that firsthand. In the sea of masked protesters, he spotted small groups of students apparently unconnected to militant organizations. “Sometimes it was four young friends, high-school or university students, probably affiliated with no network or organization, who had simply decided to come and demonstrate that way, with the intention of fighting,” he told CNN. Melchior had not seen so many people prepared for confrontation since the 2006 student riots. Police tactics are changing too Historically, France’s crowd control doctrine was all about keeping protesters at a distance. That’s become more difficult to maintain because of violent confrontations. Olivier Cappe, a former riot police officer with 25 years of experience who now represents the UN1TÉ police union, said officers are now facing threats from Molotov cocktails, fireworks mortars, pétanque balls and other projectiles. “Automatically you have to send your officers out to intervene, possibly charge and confront people,” Cappe said. “That’s where people get injured.” Staff shortages compound the problem. Cappe estimates France lacks around 800 specialist riot police officers. “The principle of French crowd control is numbers,” he said. “The more numerous you are, the more imposing you look. The more imposing you look, the less you intervene.” Outnumbered officers may resort more quickly to weapons such as rubber bullet launchers, he suggested. During both the Yellow Vest movement and more recently the student protests, officers without specialist crowd control training have been deployed with devastating results. Early in the protests, a 14-year-old boy suffered smashed teeth and a fractured jaw after a police officer fired a tear gas canister at close range, striking him in the face. A 16-year-old lost the use of an eye after being struck by a rubber bullet, while a 15-year-old lost a hand to a stun grenade, prompting the interior minister to temporarily suspend the grenade’s use. Cappe acknowledges that more forceful policing can deepen the problem. When officers confront violent groups alongside students, younger demonstrators may later come to identify with those being targeted. For student Lucas Petit, who identifies with the far left, the debate goes beyond whether violence is justified. It’s about what that violence is intended to achieve. He’s not shocked by attacks on symbols of capitalism, as he feels these acts of violence can serve a political purpose. “These are not acts of violence for the sake of violence,” he told CNN. “They have a very specific political message.” On Wednesday French President Emmanuel Macron described the escalation of violence as a collective failure. “I don’t think any high school student started pushing for their demands expecting to suffer such terrible consequences,” he said, adding police officers hadn’t signed up to face such violent confrontations either. When asked about a 15-year-old student who lost his hand, Macron said nothing could justify what had happened and reiterated his call for calm. Restoring peace to the streets is a tall order right now when so many feel that the government’s efforts to contain the violence, such as curfews, protest bans and a heavy police presence, violate their sacred right to protest and amount to a denial of democracy. And with this no longer just being a student movement, as trade unions and Yellow Vests join in, voicing grievances over the cost of living and calling on Macron to go, the anger is unlikely to subside anytime soon. On top of all that, France is heading into a deeply divisive presidential election in April, raising the stakes even further. A winter of discontent may lie ahead, with another protest on Saturday and a major demonstration scheduled for November 5, raising fears of a repeat of the extreme violence seen on October 17.

articles.title: US judge blocks Trump’s Medicaid rule forcing ill to prove impairment
articles.summary: A US district judge sided with 25 states and the District of Columbia, which sued the administration.
articles.body:
A federal judge has ruled against enforcing a new rule by the administration of US President Donald Trump that would require chronically ill people on Medicaid, a public health insurance programme for low-income individuals, to prove themselves “medically frail” to qualify for work exemptions.

US District Judge Richard Stearns blocked the rule on Thursday, siding with 25 states and the District of Columbia, which had sued the Trump administration in June over the change, arguing that it unlawfully limits exemptions for people with serious medical conditions.

The law says the definition of medically frail must include people who are blind or disabled, have substance use disorders or disabling mental disorders, have certain disabilities that significantly impair daily activities, or have serious or complex medical conditions.

But the administration’s rule went further, requiring people in those categories to show that their conditions also “significantly impair” their ability to comply with the law’s work requirements.

The plaintiffs argued that the stricter rule would prevent eligible Americans from accessing the care they need, and that it oversteps the law’s text.

“The states have met their burden of showing irreparable harm for which monetary damages would provide inadequate compensation – they face the burden of costly and intensive alterations to their eligibility verification systems,” Stearns said in his 16-page ruling.

The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, the agency that adopted the rule, declined to comment.

Medicaid is a public health insurance programme for low-income people, funded by state and federal governments.

Starting January 1, 2027, Medicaid expansion enrollees aged 19 to 64 must show that they work or do community service at least 80 hours a month, or are in school at least half the time. There are exceptions for those considered medically frail or in addiction treatment programmes, among others.

Notably, while the ruling will make it easier for some Medicaid recipients with qualifying medical conditions to obtain an exemption from the new work requirements, Stearns’s decision does not strike down the work requirements as unlawful.

Stearns serves in the District of Massachusetts and was appointed by President Bill Clinton.

His ruling upheld two other federal restrictions on how states can verify medical frailty that the states and the District of Columbia had also contested.

articles.title: Venezuela’s Machado lauds Trump for ‘freedom’, urges 2027 elections
articles.summary: Nobel winner returns to Venezuela from exile, urging elections and criticising a controversial US oil deal with Caracas.
articles.body:
Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado has thanked US President Donald Trump’s administration for opening the “floodgate to freedom” by abducting President Nicolas Maduro in January.

The Nobel Peace Prize laureate on Thursday also called for elections to be held in Venezuela next year, in her first public remarks since returning from more than 10 months in exile.

“Thanks to their vision, their courage, and their action on January 3, the floodgate to freedom has been opened,” Machado told a news conference in Caracas, naming Trump, his administration and Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

Rubio “has set out a sequence of events aimed at moving toward a democratic transition that makes clear the holding of presidential elections in 2027”, she said.

Machado has praised Trump before, presenting the president with her Nobel medal – a prize he feverishly coveted for himself in 2025.

A longtime activist, Machado fled Venezuela for Oslo in December to accept the Nobel Peace Prize. On Thursday, she said she had come home to “mobilise society”. US special forces veterans with an organisation called Grey Bull Rescue helped Machado escape by boat after she spent a year in hiding from Maduro’s regime.

Since Maduro’s abduction in January, the country has been ruled by his former Vice President Delcy Rodriguez.

Machado was greeted by cheering supporters as she travelled in her motorcade after she returned to Venezuela on Sunday. Rodriguez voiced distaste for the fanfare.

“The show could have been avoided – the airports are right here,” she said on state television.

When asked about a possible meeting with Rodriguez, the opposition leader said she had not received any message from her or from Washington.

Shortly before Machado’s statements on Thursday, Rodriguez assured the nation that elections would be held in Venezuela “with the world as witness” but did not specify a date.

Her return comes just weeks after a controversial US oil deal that will see Venezuela hand over 20 percent of its vast oil reserves.

“This agreement does not reflect the levels of transparency that Venezuelan society wants,” Machado said, criticising the deal.

articles.title: After decades of boycotts, Palestinian citizens of Israel turned out to vote. It could shape what comes next
articles.summary: For decades, many Palestinian citizens of Israel stayed away from the polls, refusing to legitimize a system they say has oppressed their people, sidelined their concerns, and failed to represent them.
articles.body: For decades, many Palestinian citizens of Israel stayed away from the polls, refusing to legitimize a system they say has oppressed their people, sidelined their concerns, and failed to represent them. But this time felt different: after four years under the most right-wing government in Israel’s history, hundreds of thousands of Arab voters decided they could not afford to sit on the sidelines. They turned out in record numbers – nearly 80% – to vote on Tuesday, compared with 53% in the last elections, according to the Mossawa Center, a civil society organization promoting equality for Palestinian citizens of Israel. That turnout gives Israel’s Arab parties unprecedented political sway with 19 seats in the 120-seat parliament. That surge was driven by a number of interlocking reasons. First, rising violent crime in the Arab community – seen as the result of negligent policing. Second, an urgent desire to oust Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and bring an end to his right-wing coalition, which includes hardline ministers such as Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich. No one was left in any doubt about the strength of feeling towards Israel’s national security minister, in particular, on Tuesday night, as chants of “Ben-Gvir, go home” broke out at the election headquarters of Joint List, the major Arab political alliance, as it became clear just how well the party had done. Long history Netanyahu’s coalition has overseen Israel’s devastating three-year war in the Palestinian enclave of Gaza, which has killed tens of thousands, and a yearslong campaign of settler violence in the occupied West Bank. “Our community wanted to bring down this criminal government, to change the grave reality caused by the policies of Netanyahu, Smotrich and Ben-Gvir,” said Dr. Ahmad Tibi, a leader of the Joint List. Tibi has spent nearly three decades urging the Arab community to exercise their right to vote. Now, he said, that high turnout is already having an impact: keeping Netanyahu from forming another right-wing government. Palestinian citizens of Israel – who make up 20% of the population – are descendants of Palestinians who were not expelled or forced to flee their homes when Israel was established in 1948. They were given citizenship but lived under military rule until 1966; many, though, feel that discrimination within Israeli society has continued to this day. They also include Palestinians who were born before 1948, like Mohammed Abdelhai’s 80-year-old aunt. On Tuesday, at her nephew’s urging, she became a first-time voter in the town of Tira, in central Israel. “I told her we have to vote,” Abdelhai said. “The last government was very aggressive with us, so this time we need every vote,” he said. The most important issue for him, he said, was a pervasive racism and lack of equality between Arabs and Jews in Israel. “If we can make a change, we can make a change. Why not? Why stay stuck in the same place?” Balance of power The strength of the Arab vote also means that neither Netanyahu’s governing coalition nor the opposition bloc are expected to win an outright majority. Now, Tibi’s Joint List, along with Ra’am, another Arab-majority party, appear to hold the balance of power. Tibi said the Joint List is prepared to help the opposition form a minority government, led by former military chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot. The Joint List would not join the government and would not seek any ministerial appointments in exchange – only a commitment to combat crime impacting the Arab community and stop the demolitions of Bedouin homes, which have risen under Netanyahu’s government. “If they want us to help, we will be there in order to help … we want to support the candidate of the opposition.” Tibi said. But doing so will require Eisenkot and his coalition to “be brave” in the face of Netanyahu’s condemnation of any attempt to form a government with the help of Israel’s Arab parties, he said. That’s because the idea of forming a government with the support of Arab parties has become politically toxic in Israel, with a majority of Jewish voters opposed. Several opposition parties have also previously ruled out such an arrangement. It remains unclear how much Eisenkot is willing to lean on the Arab parties for support. The only opposition party that supports doing that is the left-wing Democrats Party led by Yair Golan. “We have an opportunity to form a change government in partnership with Israel’s Arab citizens,” Golan said on Wednesday. “Now we need courage. We need leadership. We need to stop being afraid and to start taking action.” For Tibi, it’s more than fear holding some political leaders back. “It’s the pure racism against 20% of the population, Arab citizens. We are a legitimate part of parliament. We are a legitimate part of the citizens,” he said. Deligitimization efforts Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has consistently sought to delegitimize Arab voters and has repeatedly used the prospect of lawmakers from the Arab community sitting in government as a way to motivate his base to turn out and vote. In September, the CEC approved a motion to ban Arab parties to run in the election – a decision that was overturned by the High Court. As it became clear just how well Arab parties had polled on Wednesday, Netanyahu’s Likud issued a statement accusing them of “stealing the election.” This was followed on Thursday by the chair of Israel’s Central Elections Committee (CEC) sending a letter to the head of Israel’s security agency, the Shin Bet, asking him to investigate allegations of foreign interference in the election aimed at boosting turnout among Arab voters. In the letter, the CEC chair, Noam Sohlberg, admitted he could not attest to any of the suspicions, and Israeli police have said they have received nothing to back up the claims. Arab party leaders say Likud’s attacks amount to incitement and have pledged to defend the election results. Mansour Abbas, Ra’am party leader, said he would cooperate with any investigation and Joint List chairman Yousef Jabareen said Netanyahu was “defeated” and “refuses to accept the voters’ decision.” ‘We belong to this country’ Many of the policies that have afflicted Palestinian citizens of Israel have been enacted under Ben-Gvir, the national security minister who was previously convicted of supporting terrorism and inciting anti-Arab racism. On Tuesday, some residents in Arab-majority towns told CNN they left polling stations without voting because of intimidation from men supporting far-right Israeli parties like Ben-Gvir’s. “People face high pressure – there was an old woman who could not stand the pressure, another one is pregnant who could not bear the situation and left … this is all because of racism,” said Taibeh resident Ulfat, who asked to be identified by her first name only. From Tibi’s point of view, the higher turnout among Arab voters compared with the Jewish majority shows that Palestinian citizens are “willing to influence and take part” in Israeli politics. “We are being blocked by the right and sometimes by the opposition. This is not a democracy. It’s an ethnic democracy. It’s a democracy for Jews,” he said. That sense of exclusion was echoed by voters across Arab communities, many of whom said it is what pushed them to the polls this time. Tira resident Munther Mansour, 60, has voted in the past, but this time he sees a real chance that his vote will count. “We never took an interest in elections before. But the level of racism and changes in our day-to-day life forced people to go out and exercise their right,” he said. “We belong to this country; we are part of the country. So we must exercise this right.”

articles.title: North Korea’s Kim calls for rapid expansion of drone technology and observes weapons tests
articles.summary: North Korean leader Kim Jong Un called for rapidly expanding the country’s drone technology and observed tests of various weapons, state media reported Friday, as his nation remains embroiled in a standoff with rival South Korea along their heavily fortified border.
articles.body: SEOUL, South Korea — North Korean leader Kim Jong Un called for rapidly expanding the country’s drone technology and observed tests of various weapons, state media reported Friday, as his nation remains embroiled in a standoff with rival South Korea along their heavily fortified border. Acquiring advanced drones is a top priority for Kim, who now wants to beef up both conventional and nuclear capabilities. Experts say his troops dispatched to Russia to support its war against Ukraine have most likely gained valuable expertise on drone warfare from Russian forces and related battlefield experiences. The North’s official Korean Central News Agency said that Kim on Thursday visited an exhibition of a variety of attack and other drones that show recent achievements in the field of unmanned aeronautical technology. In a speech at the exhibition, Kim stressed the need to seize “the absolute superiority in the drone technology” and announced unspecified steps needed to “rapidly expand and strengthen the unmanned aeronautical technology,” KCNA said. To mark the event, KCNA said that North Korea later conducted test-launches of various drones, missiles and weapons from 600 mm-caliber ultra-precision multiple rocket launchers. KCNA photos showed Kim watching soaring weapons or him clenching his fist while his teenage daughter was clapping her hands beside him. South Korea’s spy agency assesses that the girl, reportedly about 13, is likely Kim’s heir. South Korea’s military earlier said it detected the launches of about 10 short-range ballistic missiles from North Korea’s eastern coastal town of Wonsan on Thursday. They were North Korea’s first ballistic weapons firings in 17 days. Tensions between the two Koreas are running high since last month’s land mine blasts at their border that wounded three South Korean soldiers. Seoul accused North Korea of burying the mines south of the military demarcation line and demanded an apology. Pyongyang has denied responsibility for the explosions and warned of retaliation if provoked. Last week, North Korea threatened to resume propaganda loudspeaker broadcasts and place new weapons systems along the border. North Korea has pulled out of talks with the U.S. and South Korea after Kim’s high-stakes diplomacy with U.S. President Donald Trump collapsed in 2019. In recent weeks, North Korea has dialed up weapons testing activities in a likely attempt to increase its leverage in potential diplomacy with the U.S. after Trump expressed his eagerness to restore talks with Kim. On Saturday, Kim made a surprise visit to a Chinese border town via a newly opened bridge and vowed to develop bilateral ties. Kim has recently taken steps to cement ties with China, North Korea’s economic pipeline, after years of prioritizing ties with Russia, including by supplying thousands of troops and ammunitions likely in return for economic and military assistance. Meanwhile, Swiss Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis arrived in North Korea on Thursday to see the reopening of Switzerland’s diplomatic office in Pyongyang and meet North Korean officials. He is traveling on to South Korea on Friday.

articles.title: At 34, Margo Fairchild built a 240-square-foot home in Virginia with her own hands; the project later helped her land a role on HGTV
articles.summary: At 34, Margo Fairchild turned a small DIY project into a home of her own, building a 240-square-foot property in Caroline County, Virginia, largely with
articles.body: At 34, Margo Fairchild turned a small DIY project into a home of her own, building a 240-square-foot property in Caroline County, Virginia, largely with her own hands. What began with making a spice rack eventually grew into a construction project that took 15 months to complete and involved everything from insulation and electrical work to designing furniture. Built during the COVID-19 pandemic, the tiny home also attracted an online following as Fairchild shared her progress. The attention helped open another door, leading to a role as co-host of HGTV's new home improvement programme, Worst Yard on the Block.How Margo Fairchild built her 240-square-foot tiny home in VirginiaFairchild did not initially set out to build an entire house. Her interest in making things developed through smaller projects, beginning with a spice rack. She wanted one that would fit her home but struggled to find a suitable option, so she decided to make it herself. That first piece of work led to building decks, and the deck projects eventually gave way to the idea of constructing a home.She had a shed shell delivered to her property in Caroline County, but the work that followed was largely her responsibility. Rather than purchasing a finished tiny house, Fairchild took on the tasks needed to turn the basic structure into a functioning living space. Her work included fitting insulation, handling electrical installations and designing the furniture.According to WTVR CBS 6 News, the finished property covers 240 square feet. Space is used carefully, with a loft bed making room for the living area below. The bathroom also has a distinctive layout, while the lounge and built-in furnishings reflect the practical decisions involved in fitting an entire home into a small footprint.Building the Virginia home during the pandemicFairchild began the project during the COVID-19 lockdown period, when restrictions and reduced social activity left her with more time at home. The construction became a long-running commitment, occupying much of her day. At certain points, she spent between 14 and 18 hours working on the property.It took around 15 months to complete the house. The process involved more than putting together the structure. Insulation, electrical work, furniture and interior arrangements all had to be addressed, requiring her to move between different aspects of construction and design.Fairchild's mother remained a source of encouragement as the project progressed, particularly when the amount of work involved became difficult to manage. Her daughter later spoke about the support she received during the building process in an interview with WTVR.Margo Fairchild's tiny home project attracted an international online followingAs the house took shape, Fairchild began posting details of the work online. Her updates attracted viewers from outside Virginia, with people in different countries following the project and offering suggestions. She recalled hearing from people in places including the Netherlands, Japan and Portland.The online audience gave her access to ideas and practical advice while she was working largely on her own. People following the construction could see the property develop from a basic shed shell into a furnished home, and the exchange gradually became part of the experience.That visibility eventually brought an opportunity beyond the house itself. Fairchild's building and DIY work helped introduce her to a wider audience, leading to a television role that connected her existing skills with a new professional project.How the tiny house project led to an HGTV hosting roleFairchild was selected to co-host Worst Yard on the Block, a new HGTV programme that focuses on improving outdoor spaces. The format brings together a master landscaper and Fairchild, who takes responsibility for builder-led projects and DIY additions intended to change the appearance and use of the yards.Her contribution centres on practical construction work rather than landscaping alone. She described her role as bringing in building skills and creating features that help improve the outdoor areas being worked on.The programme was scheduled to premiere on Wednesday, July 15, 2026, at 10:30 pm on HGTV, according to WTVR's report published on July 15 and updated the following morning.Fairchild's television work also coincided with the development of her own design business. The move from building a personal home to working on projects for a television audience marked a change in the scale of her work, although the practical skills behind both remained closely connected.From a 240-square-foot house to a new design careerThe Virginia property remains the starting point of Fairchild's story. Its construction required her to learn and carry out a range of tasks, from preparing the structure to making furniture suited to its limited floor area. The project also gave her a body of work she could share publicly, allowing people to follow her approach to building and design.Her path into HGTV did not begin with a television production or a formal career in landscaping. It grew out of a personal construction project that attracted attention online and eventually led to an opportunity to work on other people's outdoor spaces.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: Delhi traffic police announce curbs on non-BS-VI vehicles from November 1; check what's allowed, what's not
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Delhi Traffic Police has issued an advisory regarding restrictions on the entry and plying of non-BS-VI vehicles in the national capital
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Delhi Traffic Police has issued an advisory regarding restrictions on the entry and plying of non-BS-VI vehicles in the national capital from November 1, 2026, under the revised Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP) issued by the Delhi government's Environment Department on June 23, 2026.According to the advisory, vehicles below BS-VI emission standards will not be permitted to enter Delhi. BS-VI, CNG and electric vehicles will be allowed to enter the capital in accordance with the prescribed rules and exemptions.The restrictions will also apply to buses arriving from other states. Interstate diesel buses that do not meet BS-VI emission standards will not be allowed to enter Delhi.The traffic police has advised truck operators whose vehicles do not need to enter Delhi to use the Eastern or Western Peripheral Expressways or other alternative routes. Tractors and jugaad vehicles will also not be permitted to enter the capital under the applicable restrictions.Which vehicles are allowed to operate?BS-VI vehicles, CNG vehicles, electric vehicles and those exempted under the notification may operate in Delhi, subject to the applicable restrictions.Which vehicles are not allowed to operate?1. Vehicles Registered Outside Delhi:From November 1, 2026, to January 31, 2027, the entry and plying of trucks and vehicles in Delhi will be restricted, except for CNG, electric and BS-VI emission vehicles.2. Vehicles Without a Valid PUCC:Even BS-VI vehicles will not be permitted to enter Delhi without a valid Pollution Under Control Certificate (PUCC).3. Non-Destination Vehicles:Goods vehicles whose destination is not Delhi should use the Eastern or Western Peripheral Expressways or other alternative routes instead of entering the capital.4.
