articles.title: In 2025, NYU Stern professor Jim Finch pledged $10 million through a bequest for scholarships and donated $150,000 to its student investment fund
articles.summary: Jim Finch, a finance professor at NYU Stern, pledges $10 million for scholarships, with an initial $150,000 gift to enhance student investment opportunities. This donation aims to inspire others in the Stern community to contribute as well.
articles.body: The Stern School of Business is part of New York University, and scholarships funded by donations are one of the ways the university helps students cover tuition costs. NYU Stern’s alumni news says that alumni and friends give toward scholarships for many personal reasons, and that some faculty members have also established endowed scholarships for the students they teach.One recent example is Jim Finch, who teaches the Financial Services Industry class at NYU Stern and is listed on the school’s faculty page as a clinical professor of finance. NYU Stern’s alumni profile, published on June 5, 2025, reports that Finch made a $10 million bequest and jump-started it with a $150,000 cash gift to create the James S. Finch Scholarship. His giving has two parts, a long-term commitment through his estate and immediate cash gifts.Jim Finch’s path from Credit Suisse and three years of travel to the Stern faculty In the alumni profile, Finch said he retired relatively young and traveled around the world for three years before deciding he wanted to give something back. He replaced Charlie Murphy, a former Credit Suisse colleague and Stern professor, in 2016 after Murphy retired. NYU Stern’s faculty page, however, lists his start as an adjunct professor of finance in January 2018. Finch said teaching showed him how many students had scrimped and saved to reach Stern, and that he saw no reason not to help them succeed. He added that feedback from alumni who have reached their goals still comes as a bit of a shock, because it shows him how far his experience reaches.The $10 million bequest behind the James S. Finch ScholarshipThe profile’s headline describes the bequest as funding undergraduate scholarships. Because the $10 million is a bequest, it will come through his estate in the future and is not money the school currently holds. Finch said he hopes his gifts will inspire others in the Stern community to make bequests of their own. He described the school as a “giant co-op” in which everyone is a stakeholder, and said that contributing financially benefits teachers, researchers, students and the institution itself.A separate $150,000 contribution to the Investment Analysis Group’s student fund Finch also volunteers on the advisory board of the Investment Analysis Group, an undergraduate student investment club at NYU Stern. The club manages a value-focused equity portfolio that is structured as part of NYU’s endowment. The same profile says Finch made a $150,000 immediate-use contribution to the club’s investment fund to help the students grow the portfolio.That is separate from the $150,000 cash gift that started the scholarship bequest, so the profile describes two gifts of the same size, one for each purpose. Finch said he wants the club to reach a larger scale so it can add more freshmen, and he described the sophistication and thoroughness of the students’ analyses and pitches as being as strong as anything he saw in his professional career.You use AI every day. articles.body: The United States is planning to block Chinese telecom giants China Mobile, China Telecom and China Unicom from directly accessing American phone numbers, citing national security risks and concerns over scam-related robocalls.The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) said it will vote on November 19 on a proposal to restrict the companies and other IP-enabled service providers, according to Reuters.The move would also target providers using equipment from Chinese firms Huawei and ZTE, which Washington considers security threats.FCC chair Brendan Carr said the proposal would strengthen the country's defences against illegal robocallers. The agency is also considering revoking direct number authorisations for other Chinese companies it deems a national security risk and plans to bar Chinese laboratories from testing US electronics from December 2028.The move comes amid growing US concerns over Chinese cyber espionage, including the Salt Typhoon hacking campaign. Washington said the Chinese state-sponsored group stole call records and infiltrated American telecom networks in late 2024. The FBI has said the threat remains ongoing. articles.title: ‘Bravest person I know’: Father’s pride as school shooting victim leaves hospital after 262 days
articles.summary: A 13-year-old girl who was critically wounded in the deadly February school shooting in Tumbler Ridge, Canada, has been released from hospital after 262 days, her father said Thursday.
articles.body: A 13-year-old girl who was critically wounded in the deadly February school shooting in Tumbler Ridge, Canada, has been released from hospital after 262 days, her father said Thursday. “There was never a day I stopped believing we would get here. The road ahead is still long, but this is a milestone no one thought we would reach,” David Gebala wrote in an emotional social media post addressed to his daughter Maya, calling her “the bravest person I know.” Maya was among more than two dozen people wounded in the mass shooting at a secondary school in the small mining town in northern British Columbia, which left eight people dead, including six children, in the country’s deadliest school shooting in decades. She was shot three times and airlifted to British Columbia Children’s Hospital in Vancouver, where doctors initially told her family she was unlikely to make it through the night, according to Gebala. “You refused to accept the words we heard 262 days ago when you came out of the OR. Look at you, my girl. You blew every expectation out of the water,” Gebala wrote in the post to Facebook, which included a video of Maya smiling in her wheelchair. Since February, Maya has undergone five surgeries, including receiving a prosthetic skull, Gebala said in the post, which listed challenging and hopeful milestones over the past 262 days. “251 days ago, you opened your eye, moved it, and shifted your leg only to be rushed back for emergency surgery that morning,” he wrote. “179 days ago, your prosthetic skull was placed. Your fifth surgery, and the one that finally stuck.” “145 days ago, you smiled for the first time (intentionally) while we played thumb war,” Gebala went on. “61 days ago, I heard your voice again.” “Now it’s time to leave these hospital walls behind and keep moving forward, Maya Bear,” Gebala wrote, thanking the nurses, doctors and therapists “who walked every step of this with us.” Gebala has frequently offered updates on Maya’s long recovery in posts to Facebook, including a recent excursion to see the rock band Foo Fighters and celebrate her 13th birthday. Maya, who was in the school library when the massacre unfolded on February 10, was shot three times, including in the head, which shattered parts of her skull and left her with catastrophic brain injuries, according to a criminal complaint filed by her family against OpenAI. The lawsuit, filed by Maya’s mother Cia Edmonds on her behalf, is one of dozens filed against OpenAI in both US and Canadian courts on behalf of victims, survivors and witnesses accusing the tech company of negligence after it emerged that the shooter, 18-year-old Jesse Van Rootselaar, had used ChatGPT to plan the attack. The province of British Columbia is also suing OpenAI. OpenAI has pushed back against claims that it does not take safety seriously. In response to the lawsuits from the victims’ families, a company spokesperson told CNN in April that it has a “zero-tolerance policy for using our tools to assist in committing violence.” The company has said it deactivated an original account created by the shooter in June 2025 for violent activities, but Van Rootselaar made a second account to keep using the chatbot. The company’s CEO Sam Altman has previously apologized to the community of Tumbler Ridge for failing to notify authorities to the shooter’s disturbing online conversations with the AI chatbot even after staff flagged the account internally. Earlier this month, US authorities arrested a 30-year-old from Washington state who allegedly offered advice and sent money to Van Rootselaar ahead of the shooting. CNN previously reported Van Rootselaar posted about guns and hunting and her apparent mental health struggles online in the lead-up to the massacre.

articles.title: Peterborough councillor used Snapchat to catfish army cadets
articles.summary: Rylan Ray - also an Army Cadet Force volunteer - is convicted of 28 sexual offences including rape.
articles.body:
On Thursday, the 26-year-old former Conservative politician was convicted of 28 sexual offences including sexual assault and making indecent photographs of children.

Victims included children he met through his role with the Cambridgeshire Army Cadet Force. Jurors also found him guilty of raping a man.

How did a man trusted by young people and elected to represent thousands of residents come to commit such serious crimes?

It is 2022 and Ray is standing for election in Peterborough, the city he was born and raised in. One of his promises: To fight for improved safeguarding services.

With more than half of the votes, he becomes the new city councillor for Eye, Thorney and Newborough.

What residents do not know, though, is that he has already broken the safeguarding rules at the heart of his campaign – something that would ultimately lead to his downfall.

Ray, who was born Rylan Fowler, was no stranger to the Army Cadets.

He joined as a child, and was quick to return as a volunteer as an adult, rising to the rank of detachment commander.

The organisation's approach to safeguarding is clear. During Ray's trial, the jury was read a statement from head of safeguarding Nathan Ditton who said volunteers "must not send personal contact communications to a cadet in any form outside of a family relationship".

Despite that, Ray was part of a WhatsApp group for the young people in his detachment, which he said was to deter bullying.

Having access to cadets' phone numbers meant he could, and did, contact them privately.

Conversations would start professionally – praise for their good work, for example.

But he encouraged some of those conversations to move to Snapchat where they would become increasingly personal and sexual.

The app is popular with young people and messages are automatically deleted within 24 hours.

For some of the boys, they spoke to him on the app without even realising.

"Who are you?" one boy asked when a Snapchat account he did not recognise reached out to him.

It was a story echoed by other young people. Chelsie would make contact , introducing herself as a young woman from Peterborough. Some recalled her saying she was a teenager who attended a local school; others a woman in her 20s.

Chelsie would send explicit photos and videos of a woman and request similar images in return.

"That," pointing at Ray in the dock on the first day of his trial, "was Chelsie," said prosecutor Claire Matthews.

One young man grew suspicious of Chelsie and made a telephone call to a number associated with the account. The voice at the end of the phone answered: "Hello, Rylan Ray."

The court also heard how the devices linked to the account were traced back to Ray's home address in Westgate, Peterborough.

Ray's barrister Rhodri James described him as someone who "struggled to make friends and saw friendship in the wrong places".

He began caring for his mum, who attended the court for some of the trial, when he was 12.

Matthews described his behaviour as "grooming" and said he had used his fake persona to "catfish" his victims.

Catfishing, according to the Oxford English Dictionary, is the act of deceiving someone online using a fictional persona, often with the intent of luring them into a relationship.

One man, who had been contacted by Chelsie as a child, was later contacted by an account using the same name and pictures on the dating app Tinder.

Cambridgeshire Police became aware of Ray's offending after two boys made complaints at school. Three mobile phones and one laptop were seized.

A total of 704 indecent images of children were found on Ray's devices, including 73 of the most serious Category A classification.

At least five children were contacted by the Chelsie account. Not all of the children in the images found on Ray's devices have yet been identified.

Ray appeared to have deleted them from his phones but digital forensics specialists managed to extract them.

He claimed Chelsie was actually an Army cadet who he became aware was taking advantage of their colleagues and that he sent the images to his own phone so he could confront them about it.

When asked, he refused to reveal the true identity of who he believed was Chelsie.

Some boys exchanged nude photos with Ray directly.

One victim said he felt he had no choice but to comply with Ray's requests because he feared his own progression within the cadets would otherwise be hindered.

Another, who did not return images, told Ray he was not gay in an attempt to get the messages to stop. The response was: "There's a little bit of gay in everyone."

The abuse was not conducted exclusively online. Ray sexually assaulted three young people he met through the cadets and raped a man he met on a night out.

Ray also used his role as a councillor to further his relationships with teenage boys.

He had been the chairman of Peterborough City Council's licensing committee.

During the trial, one man said that while he was underage, the councillor took him on nights out in the city and that Ray's presence meant he was not asked to prove his age.

The parent of another victim said in a statement Ray took her son to parties that were attended by Ray's "acquaintances from the council".

He was removed from the council's Conservative group in February, becoming an independent member, and in May's local election he did not contest his position.

Ray also had jobs at HM Courts and Tribunals Service, the Ministry of Justice, and two schools in the Peterborough area.

At Ipswich Crown Court, it took the jury of four men and eight women about 11 hours to find Ray guilty of 23 offences. He had already pleaded guilty to five offences against one of his teenage victims.
